segments.text: So, and I head the Youth Employment and Skills team at the Africa Center for Economic Transformation. So for those who it's your first time hearing about us, we are a think tank, we're a research organization. And in my team, our entire research portfolio is focused on how to improve employment outcomes for young people and how to ensure that the skill systems at the policy level favors young people.

Now, I've been doing this for some 15 years plus and it's lovely to be back on the YouthConnekt Africa stage. And today we are going to, this is not going to be a regular session. You're all going to be very hands-on and involved.

We are about to give you a taste of what we call our Asset Youth Policy Lab. For those of you, again, it's the first time hearing about the Asset Youth Policy Lab. Every year we have about, I mean, this year when we launched it, we had about 1,200 young Africans applying to enroll in our youth policy.

And what we do is that we hack policy problems. What does that mean? We give young people a taste of what it means to be at the table when you're making policies. In my years doing this work, I come across a lot of young people who say, why don't you just fix the road? Or why don't you just address this gap? And then we sit with policymakers and they say, I can't do this because I'm constrained in A, B, C ways.

And so with this youth policy lab, we tell the policymakers and the leaders that the young people have the answers. I've seen a lot of innovative young people who come up with amazing ideas on how to solve problems that have existed for decades. And today we're going to take you through a similar exercise.

You are going to hack life in this room as policymakers and as decision makers. So today you're not going to wear the hat of just a young person. You're going to wear the hat of the person who has the money and who has the decision and who has been appointed in there.
So stick with me. I promise it's going to be an exciting session. We're going to have live voting at the end.

We're going to have teams and we're going to vote for the winners. So before we get into the live action, I have a very important person with me today that I would love to introduce. He goes by the name Honorable Laraman Yontong, who is the Deputy Minister, TVET, Ministry of Youth and Sports in Liberia.

He assumed the position in March, 2024 and he has extensive background in workforce development. Please join me with a round of applause for the Honorable Minister as he gives us our keynote address. Thank you.
Thank you. Good afternoon. I can't hear you.

Good afternoon. So let's do a little drill before I say anything. Who are familiar with the word Ubuntu? It means, it's a Swahili word that means I am because we are, right? So when I say Ubuntu, just say I am.
And when I say I am, say because we are. That's right, that's right. I know you're just coming from having lunch.
Ubuntu. Ubuntu. Ubuntu.
I am. I am. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Madam Moderator, distinguished delegates, leaders of the African Center for Economic Transformation or ACET, our vibrant young people who have been with us for quite a few days, going through different sections. I wanna say you are welcome. I would like by starting by saying that every generation of Africans has stood before a defining threshold in history.
And of course, our forefighters stood at the gate of colonialism and demanded political sovereignty. They gave us flags. They gave us national anthems.

And in some cases, they gave us seats at the table of nations. Today, our generation stand at a different, equally urgent threshold. The battle of economic sovereignty, technological self-determination, and institutional transformation.

We are the youngest generation on this planet Earth. With over 60% of our population under the age of 25 years. But we cannot build the Africa we want, or we cannot achieve the vision enshrined in the African Agenda 2063 if the true architects of the future are left out of the room.
It's not up to us to make the decisions. It's up to us to make the decisions. And this is precisely why Asset Youth Policy Lab is very important.

For me, I think it is not just an initiative, it should be a continental imperative. The Asset Youth Policy Lab is not only a dynamic platform designed to empower young Africans, but it is also meant to engage them into policy-making decisions. Through mentorship, through teamwork, through continent-wide digital campaigns, the Policy Lab has built critical skills in policy analysis, innovation, and leadership.

Amplifying the voices of young Africans to occupy spaces they are often unrepresented. More than just an idea of competition, it is a transformative learning experience that prepares Africa's next generation of leaders to shape the inclusive and sustainable future, best deserving of them. And so, distinguished delegates, let us speak with continuum about where we stand today.

We have passed the first decade of the African Agenda 2063. And while our aspirations might be soaring, structural policy gaps threaten to stall our collective march. First, in technology and digital transformation and infrastructure.

Across our continent today, millions of young innovators are ready to code, are ready to build, and are ready to trade. Yet, they are often suffocated by prohibitive data costs, fragmented regulatory frameworks, and IQ digital divide between urban spaces and rural communities. If we fail to close this policy gap, we directly undermine aspiration one of the Agenda 2063, a prosperous Africa based on inclusive growth and sustainable development.

And aspiration two, which envisages an integrated continent driven by modern infrastructure and knowledge-based economy. Second, in peace and security. Across many regions of Africa, young people are still viewed within the narrow perception of security threats, as opposed to being viewed as agents of peace.

When governance excludes youth, whether it is done inadvertently or intentionally as a structural policy design, alienation itself feeds us into instability. Leaving young people out of the early warning systems, conflict resolution, and post-conflict reconstruction directly hampers aspiration four of the African Agenda 2063, a peaceful and secure Africa. And aspiration three, which demands good governance, democracy, and respect for human rights.

Third, in development financing. You agree with me that most African young entrepreneur possess bankable ideas, yet the financial architecture remains risk-averse, collateral-heavy, and disconnected from the realities of young entrepreneurs. And so without targeted, patient capital, and youth-responsive budgeting, we cannot achieve aspiration one or aspiration seven, an Africa as strong, united, resilient, and influential global player and partner.

So fellow delegates, the important conversation that I want us to reflect on today is about how we can close the gap, the policy gap. Because closing these gaps require moving from tokenism to institutionalization. And across the continent, the tide is beginning to turn.

That's why in my home country, where I'm from in Liberia, we are proving what happens when political will meets youth agency. Our national youth program and our action plan 2025 to 2029, Liberia has intentionally mainstreamed young people into national governance and economic transformation. We are decentralizing digital hubs across all of our 15 countries.

I know some of you country, you call the preferences. We are doing that to ensure that we are bridging the gap between rural and urban tech divide. We're revamping technical and vocational education and training to ensure that job seekers are now turned into job creators.

And we are placing young professionals directly into key government ministries and decision-making portfolios. But Liberia is not alone in this. When you look across the continent, right here in Rwanda where we are today, Rwanda remains a shining example of how system work when it institutionalized youth representation, what is from the Dutch council to the national parliament.

And Kigali has positioned itself as the center of continental innovation hub. In places like Nigeria, we have heard too often of the not too young to run movement. And that movement has been able to shatter constitutional age barriers and open legislative chambers for a whole generation of young people in Nigeria.

In places like Kenya and Ghana, we are seeing how innovation is pioneering digital entrepreneurship and the entire ecosystem around youth enterprise funding and ensuring that there is a direct link, not just with innovation, but it ties into national industrial policies. These examples and many other examples across the region, tell a simple and fundamental truth, that when Africa trust its youth with power, Africa accelerates. And so today the fundamental question for all of us is what next? What must we do as we wrap up from here and go to our respective countries? One of the answers I will offer today is that we have to institutionalize platforms like the ASET policy lab into our national ministries, most especially the youth ministries.

And we have to regionalize it to the level that it is incorporated into our economic, our regional economic communities. We must mandate youth impact assessment in every national budget line. We must harmonize digital trade policies within and under the Africa continental free trade area, so that a young innovator from where I'm from in Monrovia can scale up seamlessly in Mombasa or in Nairobi or in Kigali or Johannesburg.

And finally, we must be able to de-raise financing of youth-led enterprises. Fellow Pan-Africans, the philosophy of Ubuntu teaches us that I am because we are. And in the context of the African Agenda 2063, our continent will only become what it is based on what we do to empower and build our young people.

So let's leave this gathering today not merely with stronger networks or hands-on and beautiful smiles, but let's leave with a resolution that moving forward, we'll hand the pen of policy to the generation of young people who lives are affected by the consequences of the actions that we take. The future of Africa is not waiting to be inherited. The future of Africa is ready to be co-authored.
Thank you very much. Another round of applause, please. Thank you, Honorable.

And I love the notes that he ended on, which is the future of Africa is ready to be co-authored. So young people are not just beneficiaries of policy systems and structures, but your co-creators of those policy systems and structures. So we're about to go in our business for today.
So as I said, I mean, some of you are just joining us, have a seat. It's an interactive session. I'm not going to do this by myself.
There's no panelists you're going to listen to. You are the event. So we're going to split ourselves into three groups.
Three groups. And we've already done it for you, it's random. No one in this room knew, so no one already knows the exercise, but play along and just trust me, you'll enjoy it.
So group one is all of you on that divide. You're group one. Group two, that divide.
Group two. And group three, I'm going to ask you all to come together as group three. Yes, fantastic.

So whilst that is happening, I'm going to take you through a short presentation that will provide a context of what we are going to be hacking today or the problem we're going to be hacking today. As I said, I work for an organization called Asset. We can start the slides.

Okay. And what we do at Asset, we take a research question. I mean, anyone here who has done research is like hacking, right? You collect the data, you figure out what the issue is and how to figure out how we solve that issue.

So that's exactly what we did here at Asset. We had a lot of young people in our work saying that, yeah, I'm employed, but that work is just not good enough. Who feels that way? Who here has a job, but man, you'd love a better job? Anyone here? Oh, you're all very happy in your jobs.
That's fantastic. Let me show by hand. All right.

What do we consider as a good job? Is it one that's paying well? Just say yes or no. One that's paying well? One that has social security? Health benefits? You want help maternity leave? Job satisfaction? You feel like the job is going to take you somewhere one day? You're progressing, you're seeing that you're progressing? Paternity leave for a father's young, yes, yes. Paternity leave, you want paternity leave in your jobs? And you want standard working hours, isn't it? And you want a contract that shows that I am employed by this person.

And it's not just that they can fire me the next day and I'm working overtime, I'm working ridiculous hours and I don't even have a contract. So unfortunately, that's the reality of a lot of young people on the continent. When you take the regular statistics, you hear them say it's only 9% youth unemployment rate.

And if most of you didn't know in this room, Africa has the lowest youth unemployment rate in Sub-Saharan Africa, which sometimes is shocking. But what this doesn't tell you is the nature of the jobs that young people are employed in. Often, they are not wage-paying jobs.
Why? Because young Africans are not lazy. We are very industrious. You won't find a young African sitting at home.

Either they're selling something, they're joining their parents in their business, they're going to school, they need to do something to keep going. So we said, you know what? Now the challenge is not just, ah, yes, we have 50,000 young people in jobs, but how good are those jobs? So we set out to create an index, Worker Welfare Index. And in that index, what we wanted to do was to score how good is the average job on the continent for a young worker.
We combined labor force surveys. I don't know if you know what a labor force survey is, but almost every country on the continent has it. We combined 22 African countries.
The labor force surveys for 22 African countries. A lot of our young people are still in agriculture, forestry, and fishing. That's what you're seeing on the slide.
It still employs about 34%. And that is mostly informal jobs. And then wholesale and retail trade is about nearly 10%.
You see manufacturing, you see transport, you see storage, ICT. ICT is mostly driven by South Africa. Once you take out South Africa from the data, a lot of our young people are still in there.

But then we went and looked how good are those jobs. And the indicators we used are what I was asking you in the beginning. Standard working hours, permanent contracts, written contract, paid sick leave.
Look at the number, only 35% in the data set had access to paid sick leave. It meant that when you were sick, you weren't gonna be paid. Maternity leave, only 26% of the jobs in the sample had that.
Social security, 19%. Health coverage, 18%. So that's the state of the jobs, young people.
This sample is just 18 to 35 year olds. That's the state of the jobs on the continent. So it's about time we stop looking at just jobs, but good jobs.
That's what a young African deserves. We built another index. I want to go quickly.

We built another index because each time we go to present our results, they'll ask us, but what about the employers, right? This is from labor force survey. Maybe they're lying about the quality of their jobs. Maybe the person actually earns $1,000 and they said, no, I only earn $500.

So we took data from employers to verify what we're finding. And we built another index and we called it the Employment Conditions Index. We combined data from 33,000 companies from the World Bank Enterprise Survey and it says the same thing.
The scores didn't get any better. It's still, in fact, worse than the Worker Welfare Index. So this is from the employer side.

Overall, the average score is still not good. Manufacturing, we looked at it at the sub-sector level. You see pharmaceutical, petroleum, transport turning to do a bit more better, ICT, telecommunications.

And if you have friends who work in there, you know already, they tend to be those who are doing better, have better jobs. And then you look at the weaker sides, that's in textiles, wholesale trade, retail, and that's usually our market people working in very precarious nature of jobs. So it all points to the same thing.

And one important finding for us was actually SMEs create most of the new jobs we see. But unfortunately, they don't have the systems to give you the great jobs, right? I mean, if you're working at your mom and pop shop, you can't go and say, I want health benefit. It's hard to say, you know what? Actually, I demand to be in a trade union membership when you're only two people at the job, you and the owner, right? So SMEs need better protection so that they can... So I'll wrap up this, the final slide.
So this is to give you the context. So these were the conclusions we came from that study. And we say, you know what? Invest where the jobs already are.

If we wanna lift a lot of young people out of poor jobs, let's start with where young people already work. And young people work in agriculture, in retail. So let's provide better social protection to young workers in these sectors.

And then let's grow sectors that have room for more jobs. And for us, it's about time we stop saying, when we're reporting employment, it's about time we stop saying only 9% unemployment rate. It's about time we start asking our leaders, how good are those jobs? You say you've created 100,000 jobs this year.

How good were those jobs? Was it just a tick box exercise? Can the person live on that wage? So today's exercise, which my colleague is about to hand out, we've created three simulations based on this study. You're going to hack these recommendations and tell us that if you were the leader and the policymaker, this is how I'm going to solve the problem. And the reason why I love this exercise is because as a research institute, I take this idea.

And the next time I'm sitting in front of a minister, I say, you know what? This is how young people say you should solve it. Have you considered this angle? So this is not just an exercise for an exercise sake. As I said, we're fortunate to sit in a lot of high-level meetings.
And we take your voices and we translate it into those meetings. So do not feel as though we're doing this just for the sake of doing. We're doing this.

Your voice, your suggestions, your opinions will help shape the kind of advocacy and advisory that we give to ministers when we leave this room. All right. So with that said, I'll show a short video whilst my colleague hands over.
And we'll go through how this exercise works really quickly. He has to tell me. Denzel, where are you? So that they will help us.
We don't have much time. No. So where is the other exercise? So take it out and hand it over to them.
We don't have much time. So which is group three? Yeah, so I have to look at it. Ah, Denzel.
So you see when you do this. Yeah, but you should have sorted it. So where is D2? So where is D2 and D3? This is D1.
Yes, so give them D3. And where is D2? So give it to her so she can. Sorry, just a second.
You can turn around. Those in the front seat, turn around. Face your group.
Fantastic. So in front of you, you have a sheet that tells you what your simulation is. And as I said, now we're talking about not just jobs, but good quality jobs.
So we're going to give you about 30 minutes. I know usually policymakers have a lot more time. But we're challenging you because we know you're super smart.
And you're faster. And you're wittier. Right? So you're going to get 30 minutes to hack it.
Imagine you're the minister. They come and sit in front of you. And then they say, look, this is the situation.
And on the paper, you will read it. This is the, if any francophone speakers are around. We have a French version.
So you can just, do you have the French version? Okay, great. Any other francophones? We have a French version we can give you. Great.
So we'll give you about three minutes. Read it. And very quickly, again, this happens in real life, where you have to work with people very quickly.
So you will nominate who will present your pitch. Because at the end of this, there will be a live pitch. If you've done a pitch before, you have five minutes to present your idea and make it sell.
Because all of us here are going to be judges. All of us here at the end are going to be judges. Right? So choose one person who will be your pitch lead.
The person will pitch at the end. And we will all vote for which of the ideas is the best. So good luck.
Myself, Mona, my colleague Denzel, we will come around. And we will take any questions you have, if anything is not clear. Thank you.
Also, it's usually a good idea to appoint a timekeeper. Someone who sets their timer for 30 minutes. And I just don't know why.
So Okay, teams, we've got 10 minutes left. And at this stage, you should be thinking of who is going to pitch. You can volunteer, your team can select.

Start thinking of who is going to stand on this stage and pitch to everyone what your idea to your problem is. And as you're thinking about your pitches, I want you to remember to open with what the scenario is. Because everyone is hacking a different problem.

So make sure you open with just a summary of what your problem is and what you're hacking. You're free to take notes and come on stage with your notes so that you can read from your notes. But you have got 10 minutes.
And then we start the live pitch. And let me remind you, you have just five minutes for the pitch. So you sell your idea as an elevator pitch.
You're in the elevator with the head of AU. You need to sell your idea and sell it quick. Okay, my people, are we ready? Are we ready? Are my pitches ready? Five more minutes.

The job isn't easy, huh? It's not easy, yeah? And guess what? These are real-life scenarios of some of how the countries are faced with multiple constraints. So policymaking isn't always easy. Okay, five more minutes.

And then I want my pitches to get ready. So Denzel is going to come around and take the name of the person who is going to pitch. And anything else you want me to add when I announce you? You can even come up with a team name.
Okay, two more minutes now. Two more minutes. All right, it's officially time to pitch.
Are we ready? All right, I would love to see you all. Let's just quickly rearrange the chairs to face back to plenary. Let's face the stage.

My group here, group three, I will encourage all of you to move here so that we can just all face, yeah. Okay, and group four as well, if we can move to the front of the room, that way we can all face the audience. Are we ready? Denzel, let me have my names of the pitches.
I'm excited. No, I'm excited. We want answers, we want solutions, and we want it now.

All right, so for group one, oh, I would love to know which countries they come from as well. So group one, we have Molefo Lesotho, right? Did I guess right? Okay, fantastic. Group two is represented by Seleki.
Did I mention it correctly? Seleki. Is it Crema? Which country? Liberia. Okay, wow.

Joy and Delia, let me see you up on the stage. And finally, for group four, we've got Lolia. Is that correct? Lolia, can I see you up on the stage? And as I said, let's move to the front of the room.
Okay, drum roll. Are we excited? Each group has five minutes to pitch. You all just met each other 30 minutes ago, so this has not been easy to hack and to hack that quickly.
So before we go into the pitches, I want us to give ourselves a huge round of applause for making it this far. Let me hear you. I think you need to clap for yourselves even louder and even better.
Let's go again. Yes. You know, you could have walked out of that room, but you stayed and you did the exercise and you did the simulation.
So that's something to be proud of. Is it ladies against gents? Okay, we're waiting for one more person, Lolia. So Lolia will be presenting for the Francophone group.

So we've got translating equipment behind there. If you're not bilingual, cannot speak French, please grab a headset. The reason is because you're all voting and we wouldn't want you to vote them low because you didn't hear what they said or you didn't understand what they said.
So please grab a headset. We've got translation available so that you can be a fair judge. Denzel, I think we're still missing Lolia.
Denzel, can I have the judges brief? Okay, people. I'm missing Lolia. Did Lolia change her mind? Or is Lolia coming? Okay, I think Lolia is coming.
I'm hoping Lolia is coming. Okay, so judges. Now you were, five minutes ago you were hackers.
Now you're all going to be judges. So I'm going to take a few minutes to read what you need to do as a judge. Are you ready? So as a judge, you're going to vote our pitches on the following things.
You're going to vote based on how well they used any type of evidence. That's if they did. If they didn't, it's fine.
I presented some evidence earlier on as clues. If anyone found the use for it, sure. But if not, it's fine.

How good the result is, right? So as a judge, I want you to be thinking through how good was it? How feasible was it? So think through when you're listening to the pitches, how feasible it is. And does it have an inclusion lens? Do you find that the solution serves everyone well? You know, because we always, as young people, when we're programming, we need to think about excluded groups. And the potential to scale the solution.
How feasible is it going to be that you roll this out on a large scale? So these are the things you should consider as a judge. And no favoritism. Don't vote for your team to win.
Vote for the right idea. I know I'm in a room filled of young people who are credible and integrity. So I'm going to count on you.
All right, so with that said, we are going to go into our pitches. Are we ready? Are we ready? You're not? Give them a round of applause. Ginger them.
All right, so group one, are we ready? I'm going to set the timer of five minutes. Denzel, help me with that. And you can stand.
You can do what you need to do to make it easier for you. Are we ready? Molefe, are you ready? Group one. All right, the floor is yours.

Good afternoon, everyone. I am Molefe from Lesotho and we are in group one. Now, the challenge that we have recognized and we will be working with is in agriculture, where there's only agriculture was scored with 37.8% on the weakest conditions for employees.

Now, in trying to understand this problem or even attempting to address it is to say, we need to recognize that improving these conditions requires both contributions of the employers as the farmers, as well as the employees and the larger ecosystem that exists around them and their products. So, as we framed this, we want to say, we need to work towards creating policies that embrace Ubuntu, the humility in the way employers treat their employees. Because employees thrive where they feel valued, where they feel that they are appreciated.

Despite or regardless of the earnings that they are getting. But because of that Ubuntu concept, employees can feel more empowered. Therefore, the first intervention that would be put in place within this 180 days would be training employers on how to treat employees with respect and humility.

Then secondly, to solidify this would be to have a policy that requires employers to work with the employees to establish contracts of how they are going to even work. Then within these contracts, this is where we can talk about minimum wages. We can talk about leave days, whether maternal or paternal.

We can talk about even just how we communicate. Because the great innovation thrives where people feel appreciated. And therefore, if we want to grow or foster that, we must go at the grassroots of it.

Now, beyond that is to help these employers, that is the farmers, to have an enhanced value add in what they are producing by helping them connect or have a larger ecosystem in which they trade amongst themselves. So if the government was to act or serve as a liaising body, that allows the farmers to meet the market and ensure that it breaks the barriers from production to the demand of the market by having standardized targets on what quality is that is required. And ensuring that it allows or creates a platform where these two parties, being the farmers as well as the market, can collectively decide on what is needed and how best they can achieve that.

I think in doing so can be simple and we can celebrate the small wins or set a monitoring and evaluation plan to say, have we established a platform where the farmers, the employees, as well as, in fact, the farmers and the employees have established contracts on how they work. Have we then also marked whether these farmers have had training that allows them to be compassionate and empathetic in how they treat their employees. And beyond that, then we would say, have we also established a platform where the farmers and- All right, we are out of time.
A round of applause. A round of applause for Molefe. Did you hear the pitch? You need to pay attention because you're judges.

Yes, so Molefe just presented on how they are going to improve conditions in agriculture. And he had solutions for both employers, employees, and the role that governments will serve as a bridge to getting this done. So another round of applause.
Next, we have group two, which is Seleke. From Liberia. A round of applause.
You're free to stand. This is your audience, Seleke. Over to you.
Hello, everyone. I'm Seleke Komar, a proud Liberian. And I'm here representing the Liberian community in Rwanda.

In this exercise, I'm representing group two. So we are basically working on how we can bring informal sector or informal workers into social security and health coverage in a way that they can afford. So first of all, let's look at what those, you know, that we consider informal workers.

These are basically motorcyclists, taxi drivers, mechanics, freelancers, gig workers, that most of them earn on a daily basis, weekly, you know. And you know what it means to be earning daily, weekly, and want to, you know, contribute to social security as compared to someone in informal sector where they earn on a monthly basis. So how can we bring these people to contribute to social security, you know? So that's the problem basically we're trying to solve.
So we're able to come up with five solutions. And number one is pay as they earn. So like the formal workers, they can contribute to social security based on what they earn.

So some of them, they earn on a daily basis. So it's not fair to say they contribute to social security on a monthly basis when they earn daily, you know. Some of them earn weekly or maybe after two weeks or three weeks or something like that.

So it's better as they earn on a daily basis, they can make a contribution towards that social security. So number two is mobile money integration. And I think for those of you who live here in Rwanda, you've experienced whatever you do here is done through mobile money transaction.

So you can try to integrate that same kind of system where they use their mobile phones, you know, to do these different payment without physically going to deposit, you know, the payment that they can contribute to social security. Three, we have affordable health coverage. So now people in the informal sector cannot be charged, you know, with the same fees as compared to people in the formal sector because they don't earn the same, you know.

So you have to make things easier for people in the informal sector, make it feel affordable. And based on their income, you know, what they are earning, whether it is daily, weekly, or monthly or whatsoever. So you make it affordable for them.

And then the fourth, government and private sector support where you have government providing subsidies for low income workers, telecom companies and digital platform have facilitated these different contributions. And then the employees, cooperative and gig workers platform contribute to small percentage on behalf of registered workers where applicable. Now, how can we implement these things? We propose also a simple five-step approach.

Number one, registration, where your informal or gig workers register through mobile apps, cooperative market associations and local community organization. Number two, identification. You give each registration a registered worker or digital social security account linked to that phone number.

Three, flexible payment. You allow contributions starting from small affordable amount, depending on workers earning. Fourth, obviously government partnership where, you know, you work with relevant ministries, social security institution, health insurance providers and mobile money companies.

Last but not the least, which is five, you educate your workers about the importance of saving their future healthcare and social potential. Now, what impact do we expect? The impact we expect from this increased access to health insurance among young informal workers, financial protection against unexpected illness and emergency. Okay, Seliki, it's time.
Thank you. A round of applause. A round of applause.
It's not easy to come up with these great ideas in 30 minutes. So well done, group two. A round of applause for Seliki.
All right, ladies, are we ready? Are we ready? Joy and Delia are going to represent group three. Over to you, ladies, your audience. All right.
Okay, it's audible. All right, good afternoon, everyone. My name is Unyandisa Joy Kuhepa Hengari.

I am from Namibia, representing the National Youth Council of Namibia. But for this exercise, I am representing group three and we are focusing on training. So among formal firms, the employment condition index averages 0.3 with training one of its weakest spots.

So as group three, we were focusing on, all right, so in terms of training, how can we mitigate this area? How can we have standardized training for the continent?
